links.note: An eighth-century Irish monk on the Continent, mixing fact with legend, traced the Irish daily office to Antony, Paul, Macarius and other early hermits. Warren, who edited the Bangor Antiphonary in 1895, judged this single late account sound at its core but wrong in detail. He held that any Eastern features reached Ireland through Gaul.

links.note: Jonas of Bobbio, writing around 640, tells how Columbanus sailed from Ireland and founded Luxeuil in Gaul. Local nobles then founded monasteries under his rule, among them Donatus, bishop of Besançon, and Dado at Rebais. The handbook of penances Columbanus wrote on the Continent became a model for later Frankish ones.

links.note: Writing to Pope Gregory around 600, the Irish monk Columbanus cited Gildas, the British monk and writer. He reported that a writer named Vennianus had asked Gildas about monks who left their monasteries, and that Gildas answered most elegantly.

sources.work: Columbanus, Letter to Pope Gregory, NPNF II.13
sources.quote: The author Vennianus enquired about these of Giltas, who replied to him most elegantly

sources.work: Columbanus, Letter to Pope Gregory, NPNF II.13
sources.quote: those monks who for a closer sight of God, or inflamed by a longing for a more perfect life, going against their vows, leave the places of their first conversion

links.named_in_text: british-welsh-christianity relationsSummary, as rewritten in prose change 3 (the old text said only 'distinct from Irish Christianity')
wants: The Gildas fragments as cited by Columbanus, and the Irish catalogue of saints that names him, to show the wider Irish reception the corpus map flags as needs-ruling
drafter_flags: The letter also cites 'the writer Giltas' on simoniac bishops (line 4513-4514), but an XML endnote sits inside that sentence, so it cannot be quoted cleanly.
Vennianus is usually identified as Finnian; the vendored text does not say who he was, so the note does not.

Patrick, a Briton by his own account (Confession 1, 23), is the other possible line from the British church to Ireland; neither text names it as a relationship and his dates are disputed, so nothing drafted.
links.change_reason: New: replaces a 'distinct from' statement, which no link type expresses, with the documented contact between the two churches.

links.note: Bede records two meetings around 603 between Augustine of Canterbury and the British bishops, the first at Augustine's Oak. Pope Gregory had placed the British bishops under Augustine, but at the second meeting they refused to accept him as archbishop. Bede wrote this account more than a century later.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), II.2, chapter title
sources.quote: and of the vengeance that pursued them for their contempt, [a.d. 603.]

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), II.2
sources.quote: Augustine, with the assistance of King Ethelbert, drew together to a conference the bishops, or doctors, of the next province of the Britons, at a place which is to this day called Augus- tine's Ac, that is, Augustine's Oak

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), II.2
sources.quote: They answered they would do none of those things, nor receive him as their archbishop

sources.work: Gregory the Great, answers to Augustine (Register XI.64), question IX, NPNF II.13
sources.quote: But of all British bishops we commit the charge to thy Fraternity, that the unlearned may be taught, the weak strengthened by persuasion, the perverse corrected by authority.

links.named_in_text: british-welsh-christianity relationsSummary ('older than the Gregorian mission it later met; rejected Augustine's authority'), longDescription ('When Augustine of Canterbury arrived from Rome and met British bishops around 603') and why
drafter_flags: Party choice: the inventory matched 'Gregorian mission' and Augustine to roman-church-gregorian. I placed the meeting with anglo-saxon-christianity, because that entry dates itself from Augustine's landing in 597 and Augustine met the Britons as bishop in Kent. Gregory himself never met or wrote to the British bishops; his letter is cited for the authority at issue. The reviewer should confirm the party.
Bede's chapter carries legendary matter (the hermit's test, the healed blind man, the prophecy fulfilled at Chester). The meetings and the refusal are the core the note uses.
The Responsa (Register XI.64) is the letter Bede also quotes (I.27); its 'XI.64' number is from the NPNF heading region, not re-checked against Ewald-Hartmann.
links.change_reason: New: the British text names the meeting and the refusal twice; no link existed.

links.note: Augustine's successor Laurentius wrote to the British clergy, urging them into Catholic unity. Aldhelm later wrote a book against their Easter reckoning, Bede reports. Bede himself complained that the Britons, who would not share the faith with the English, still held to their errors.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), II.4
sources.quote: The same Laurentlus and his fellow bishops wrote a letter to the priests of the Britons, suitable to his rank, by which he endeavoured to confirm them in Catholic unity

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), V.18
sources.quote: Aldhelm, when he was only a priest and abbdt of the monastery of Malmesbury, by order of a synod of his own nation, wrote a notable book against the error of the Britons, in not celebrating Easter at the proper time

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), V.22
sources.quote: the Britons, who would not acquaint the English with the knowledge of the Christian faith, now, when the English people enjoy the true faith, and are thoroughly instructed in its rules, continue inveterate in their errors

links.named_in_text: british-welsh-christianity longDescription ('they declined to accept his authority or to join his mission to the Saxons') and why ('keeping their own dating of Easter'): the refusals the English church wrote against
wants: Aldhelm's letter to Geruntius (Geraint), king of Dumnonia, on the British Easter and tonsure, which is the book Bede means
drafter_flags: Second link on this pair; each is separately evidenced (the 603 meetings in II.2; the later polemic in II.4, V.18 and V.22).
Named-in-text is indirect: the British text names what the British refused, not the English writing against it. The reviewer may prefer a short prose addition.
Laurentius's letter to the Irish bishops in the same chapter (lines 3838-3857) is an English act against the Irish church as well; not drafted, since neither text names it.
links.change_reason: New: the English church's written case against the British church, by name, across a century.

links.note: In his history of the English church, Bede cites Gildas as the Britons' own historian for their sins after the Romans left. Bede then adds a charge of his own: that the Britons never preached the faith to the English.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation (Giles/Jane 1903), I.22
sources.quote: which their own historian, Gildas, mournfully takes notice of, they added this — that they never preached the faith to the Saxons, or English, who dwelt amongst them

drafter_flags: Bede names Gildas once. His wider reuse of Gildas in I.12-16 is standard scholarship but is not shown by any vendored or repo-cited source; the note claims only the citation.
'After the Romans left' rests on the chapter's context (I.22 opens with the Britons 'for a time delivered from foreign invasions', line 1760) rather than on the quoted lines.
links.change_reason: New: the British legacy names Gildas reaching Bede; Bede's citation documents it.

links.note: At the third council of Toledo in 589, the Gothic bishops condemned the faith they had held, which the council called Arian. They cursed anyone still keeping communion coming from Arius, and the booklet issued in King Leovigild's reign to bring Romans over to it. Eight bishops, Ugnas and Murila among them, signed as men entering the catholic church.

sources.work: Third Council of Toledo (589), anathema 1, Collectio canonum Ecclesiae Hispanae (Madrid, 1808)
sources.quote: Omnis ergo, qui fidem et communio- nem ab Ario venientem, et hucusque a no- bis retentam adhuc tenere desiderat et de to- ta.cordis intentione non damnat, anathe- ma sit.

sources.work: Third Council of Toledo (589), anathema 16, Collectio canonum Ecclesiae Hispanae (Madrid, 1808)
sources.quote: Quicumque libellum detestabilem duodecimo anno Leovigildi regis a. nobis editum, in quo continetur Romanorum ad haeresem Arianam transductio

links.note: A Latin chronicle written in Spain in 754 records how the Muslim army ended the Gothic kingdom and made it tributary. It names Urbanus of the see of Toledo and its archdeacon Evantius among the men who strengthened the church under the new rulers. Its editor notes that the chronicler traced the bishops of Toledo almost to his own time.

prose_changes.old: Contested line from Gallic/Eastern asceticism; parent of Anglo-Saxon Christianity
prose_changes.new: A thinly documented line from Gallic and, through Gaul, Eastern asceticism; one of the two roots of Anglo-Saxon Christianity
prose_changes.reason: 'Contested' did not match the evidence or the links: both inherited lines are Inferential-Thin, resting on one eighth-century tract and Warren's reading that the East reached Ireland 'through a Gallican channel' (antiphonary 1572-1576). No source argues the other side. 'Parent' narrowed to 'one of the two roots', as the Anglo-Saxon entry itself has two.

prose_changes.old: Irish monasticism reshaped continental Christianity: Columbanus's foundations seeded dozens of monasteries across Gaul and Italy, and Iona-trained missionaries carried the faith into Northumbria and beyond. The penitential handbooks written here spread through the Frankish church and stand behind the private, repeatable confession that became normal Western practice. Its scriptoria produced the insular manuscript style that culminates in the Book of Kells, and the high crosses and round towers of Irish monastic sites are among the most recognizable Christian monuments anywhere. Iona, Clonmacnoise and Glendalough are all still visited, and Iona has a working religious community again.
prose_changes.new: Irish monks left their mark far beyond Ireland. Columbanus founded Luxeuil in Gaul and Bobbio in Italy, and nobles in Gaul founded many more monasteries under his rule. Iona-trained missionaries carried the faith into Northumbria and beyond. The handbook of penances Columbanus wrote on the Continent became the model for a long line of Frankish ones. Its scriptoria produced the insular manuscript style that culminates in the Book of Kells. The high crosses and round towers of Irish monastic sites are among the most recognizable Christian monuments anywhere. Iona, Clonmacnoise and Glendalough are all still visited, and Iona has a working religious community again.
prose_changes.reason: 'Dozens of monasteries' and 'reshaped continental Christianity' go beyond Jonas (five named houses under the rule) and the Cursus tract ('multa coenobia'). The penitential that shaped the Frankish ones was written on the Continent, not in Ireland (Wasserschleben 1851); the claim about private, repeatable confession has no vendored or repo-cited source and is cut. One long sentence split in two; the rest unchanged.

prose_changes.old: The church the Anglo-Saxon invasions displaced - distinct from Irish Christianity, older than the Gregorian mission it later met; rejected Augustine's authority (603) and did not conform at Whitby (664)
prose_changes.new: The older church of Roman Britain, pushed west by the Anglo-Saxon invasions. Separate from the Irish church, though Irish monks cited its writer Gildas. It met Augustine's mission around 603, refused his authority, and kept its own Easter long after Whitby (664)
prose_changes.reason: 'Distinct from Irish Christianity' is a cataloguing statement; replaced with the documented separation and contact (Bede II.4; Columbanus citing Gildas). 'Did not conform at Whitby' implied the British were present; Bede's list shows they were not, and Bede V.22 and the Annales Cambriae show their Easter kept until 768. 'Gregorian mission' becomes 'Augustine's mission', which the link places with the English church.

prose_changes.old: There is no separately continuing British church: its dioceses were gradually drawn into the wider Western church, and the Welsh bishops came under Canterbury's authority in the twelfth century. What it left is written across the landscape. The llan- place names of Wales mark its churchyards, its founder-saints are still the dedications of Welsh and Cornish parishes, and its inscribed memorial stones survive in numbers. Gildas's account, for all its fury, became the foundation of what later writers thought they knew about post-Roman Britain, reaching Bede and everyone after him. And Brittany, settled from Britain in these centuries, kept both a Celtic language and a cluster of British saints' cults that are still there.
prose_changes.new: There is no separately continuing British church. The Welsh church carried on under its own bishops after 768, and was gradually drawn into the wider Western church. What it left is written across the landscape. The llan- place names of Wales mark its churchyards, its founder-saints are still the dedications of Welsh and Cornish parishes, and its inscribed memorial stones survive in numbers. Gildas's account, for all its fury, reached Bede, who cited him as the Britons' own historian. And Brittany, settled from Britain in these centuries, kept both a Celtic language and a cluster of British saints' cults that are still there.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited source for the Welsh bishops coming under Canterbury in the twelfth century; cut, and the continuation after 768 stated instead (Annales Cambriae, Elbodug d. 809 as archbishop). 'Reaching Bede and everyone after him' narrowed to what Bede I.22 shows.

prose_changes.old: The Visigoths ruled Spain as Homoian Christians for over a century, in uneasy coexistence with the Nicene population they governed — until King Reccared announced his own conversion and, at the third council of Toledo in 589, brought the Gothic bishops with him. Nothing quite like it happened anywhere else: a kingdom's own church council formally abandoned its creed and adopted its subjects'. What followed was one of the more remarkable intellectual efforts of the early Middle Ages. Isidore of Seville set out to gather what survived of classical learning into a single encyclopedia, and his circle — his brother Leander, Braulio of Zaragoza, Ildefonsus of Toledo — produced letters, liturgy, histories and rules around him. The councils of Toledo worked as something between a synod and a parliament, legislating for church and kingdom together, and their record also includes a harsh and escalating body of law against Spain's Jews. All of it ended abruptly with the Muslim conquest of 711.
prose_changes.new: The Visigoths ruled Spain as Homoian Christians for over a century, in uneasy coexistence with the Nicene population they governed — until King Reccared announced his own conversion and, at the third council of Toledo in 589, brought the Gothic bishops with him. Nothing quite like it happened anywhere else: a kingdom's own church council formally abandoned its creed and adopted its subjects'. What followed was one of the more remarkable intellectual efforts of the early Middle Ages. Isidore of Seville set out to gather what survived of classical learning into a single encyclopedia, and his circle — his brother Leander, Braulio of Zaragoza, Ildefonsus of Toledo — produced letters, liturgy, histories and rules around him. The councils of Toledo worked as something between a synod and a parliament, legislating for church and kingdom together, and their record also includes a harsh and escalating body of law against Spain's Jews. The Gothic kingdom fell abruptly to the Muslim conquest of 711, though its church lived on under the new rulers.
prose_changes.reason: 'All of it ended' contradicted the legacy field. The Chronicle of 754 shows the kingdom made tributary and the see of Toledo still served after the conquest (chronica-minora-2 33856-33860, 34480-34490).
